q: Which statement is the binary-search-tree property?
options: Every key in a node's left subtree is smaller, and every key in its right subtree is larger
Each node is smaller than both of its children
Each node's left child is smaller and its right child is larger (only the children are compared)
All leaves are at the same depth
explain: The property is about whole subtrees, not just the two children. Comparing only children can accept trees that are not BSTs. 'Smaller than both children' is the min-heap property.

q: An inorder traversal of a binary search tree lists its keys…
options: in the order they were inserted
level by level from the root
explain: Inorder visits the left subtree (all smaller keys), then the node, then the right subtree (all larger keys), so the output is sorted.

q: The keys 15, 10, 20, 8, 12, 17, 25 are inserted in that order into an empty BST. What is the postorder traversal?
explain: The tree has root 15, left child 10 (children 8, 12) and right child 20 (children 17, 25). Postorder is left, right, node: 8 12 10, then 17 25 20, then 15.

q: The keys 1, 2, 3, …, n are inserted into an empty BST in increasing order. What is the height of the tree (in edges)?
explain: Each new key is larger than everything so far, so it becomes the right child of the previous one. The tree is a chain of n nodes, which has n − 1 edges from root to leaf.

q: To delete a node that has two children, the standard method replaces its key with…
options: its inorder successor: the smallest key in its right subtree
the key of its left child
the largest key in the whole tree
explain: The inorder successor is the next key in sorted order, so putting it in the deleted node's place keeps the BST property. The successor has no left child, so deleting it is an easy case. The inorder predecessor works equally well.

q: Where in a BST does a newly inserted key always end up?
options: As the parent of the smallest key
Wherever there is free space on the lowest level
explain: Insertion searches for the key and attaches it where the search falls off the tree, which is always a new leaf. (Splay trees, topic 4, then move it to the root.)

q: What is the worst-case time to search an unbalanced BST with n keys?
explain: Search costs O(h). In the worst case, for example after sorted insertions, the tree is a chain with h = n − 1.

q: How many structurally different binary search trees can hold the three keys 1, 2, 3?
explain: Root 1: 2 shapes for {2, 3}. Root 2: 1 shape. Root 3: 2 shapes for {1, 2}. Total 2 + 1 + 2 = 5, the Catalan number C₃.

q: Where is the smallest key in a non-empty BST?
options: At the leftmost node: keep going left from the root
At the leftmost leaf of the bottom level
explain: Every left step leads to smaller keys. The node with no left child at the end of that walk is the minimum. It need not be a leaf, because it may have a right child.

q: In a BST, the inorder successor of a node that has two children never has a left child.
explain: True. The successor is the leftmost node of the right subtree. If it had a left child, that child would be smaller and would be the successor instead.
